Brick 5, step by step

This page shows, with short animations made for this course, everything your team does in Lab 05: the interview, the SRS-Lite, the use-case model, the domain model, the first function-point count — then the hour at home. The full conditions are in the lab document; this page is the visual companion.

Time budget 1 – 2 – 11 h lecture · 2 h in class · 1 h at home — at most 3 hours of lab work (2 in class + 1 at home)
Deliverable/docs/05-srs.md + diagrams in /docs/img/, tag block5, link and tag on the LMS (Learning Management System)
DueSunday, December 20, 2026, 23:59 — recommended first version block5-draft by Sunday, October 25, 23:59
Weight6.5 % of the course grade, the four Cs: Complete · Correct · Consistent · Clear

Every tool and technique here is open. The interview script, the requirement pattern, the use-case template, the CRC (Class–Responsibility–Collaborator) cards, the drawing tool, the spreadsheet, Git, the hosting site, the editor — each is a suggestion. Replace any of them, combine them, or build your own: a function-point counter, a verifiability checklist, a use-case form. Research what you choose — who makes it, its licence and price, where your data goes — and name it in section 0 of your file. Starting points (official sites): Git1 · GitHub2 · GitLab · Codeberg · Visual Studio Code4 · Mermaid3 and the Mermaid Live Editor8 · PlantUML · draw.io5 · Excalidraw5 · Python6.

Before you open a link or install anything, use the checklist of the Legal Notice, section 14 and Annex C: official sites only, links checked with VirusTotal, published checksums verified.

How to use the animations. They play by themselves. Pause freezes the last frame (the complete result), Restart plays from the beginning, a click on an animation enlarges it (on a phone it turns sideways), and the two download buttons save the animation or its last frame for your notes. A red number such as 1 points to a version note: tools change, and a newer version may look different from what you see here. In class — Studio 1:10–2:50, wrap-up to 3:00

1

Set up — the fence, the harms, the stories

1:10–1:20 · 10 minutes · in class

  1. Copy 05-srs_TEMPLATE.md to /docs/05-srs.md; fill the header; name the Scribe; start the timer.
  2. Copy the scoping decision of Brick 3 word for word — it is the fence around everything you write today.
  3. Name two or three harms: who is hurt, how. They become your security and privacy requirement in Step 3.
  4. Write six to eight user stories (US-01 …): As a ⟨role⟩, I want ⟨something⟩ so that ⟨benefit⟩.

Done when: header, fence, harms and six stories are in the file.

2

Interview your users — the partner team

1:20–1:40 · 20 minutes · in class

  1. Prepare (4 min): six questions — two open, two closed, two probing. Name the interviewer and the note-taker.
  2. Interview A (6 min): you ask your partner team about your product. Ask about their day, not about your solution.
  3. Interview B (6 min): swap roles.
  4. Debrief (4 min): the six questions, the three most useful answers and one surprise go into section 1. Inside the fence → a story; outside → parked.

No photos or recordings of your partners without their permission — Legal Notice, section 17. Fictional names in the file (sections 6.7 and 18.2).

Done when: section 1 holds six questions, three answers and one surprise.

3

SRS-Lite — requirements that can be tested

1:40–2:10 · 30 minutes · in class

An SRS (Software Requirements Specification), in a short form: every line written so that a test could pass or fail it.

  1. Functional requirements (15 min): 8 to 12, FR-01 onwards — ID · "The system shall …" · source · how we verify it. One behaviour each; no solutions.
  2. Non-functional requirements (10 min): exactly five, one per category — performance (a number and a condition), security or privacy (from the harms), usability (measurable), reliability, maintainability.
  3. Constraints (5 min): three — platform, technology, time, law or money.

Structure borrowed from ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (joint standard 29148 of the International Organization for Standardization, the International Electrotechnical Commission and the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers: requirements engineering), in a "Lite" subset.

Done when: 8–12 FRs, 5 NFRs and 3 constraints, each with an ID, a source and a verification line.

4

Use-case model — the map, then the detail

2:10–2:30 · 20 minutes · in class

  1. Actors (3 min): every role that uses the product, plus external systems.
  2. Diagram (7 min): at least five use cases named verb + object, connected to their actors, inside one system boundary — on paper, in draw.io or Excalidraw, in PlantUML, or as Mermaid text.3
  3. Two fully-dressed use cases (10 min): actor, trigger, preconditions, main flow (actor does / system does), at least two alternative flows each, postconditions. The third is written at home.

The fully-dressed template comes from Alistair Cockburn, Writing Effective Use Cases (2001); the diagram notation from the OMG (Object Management Group) UML (Unified Modeling Language) specification.

Done when: the diagram shows ≥ 5 use cases and all actors; two use cases are fully dressed.

5

Domain model — CRC cards, then a class diagram

2:30–2:45 · 15 minutes · in class

  1. CRC round (7 min): one index card per noun the product must remember — name, responsibilities, collaborators. Throw away screens, buttons, databases, controllers. Keep 5 to 8.
  2. Class diagram (8 min): one box per surviving card with 2–4 attributes; every association with a verb and multiplicities at both ends. Mermaid text inside the file (GitHub draws it), or an image in /docs/img/.

Done when: 5–8 analysis classes with attributes; every association labelled; no design classes.

6

A first function-point count

2:45–2:50 · 5 minutes · in class (checked at home)

  1. Go down the FR list and tick each element: EI (external input), EO (external output), EQ (external inquiry), ILF (internal logical file), EIF (external interface file).
  2. Weights 4 · 5 · 4 · 10 · 7 → UFP (unadjusted function points).
  3. FP (function points) = UFP × (0.65 + 0.01 × ΣF), with ΣF = 35 → × 1.00.

The method is maintained by the IFPUG (International Function Point Users Group); the course uses a simplified, average-weight version.7

Done when: five counts, the UFP line and the FP line are in the file.

Wrap-up 2:50–3:00. Exit ticket, one sentence on paper: “One requirement you rewrote to make it testable — before and after.” Commit and push before you leave — a file in the repository is safe and can be reviewed; a file on one laptop is neither.

At home — 60 minutes, maximum

7

The third use case, and the alternative flows

15 minutes · at home

Fully dress the third use case. Then read all three as a tester: at every step, what if this fails? A full slot, a lost connection, a wrong password — each answer the product must handle becomes an alternative flow, and each alternative flow that needs a requirement gets one.

Done when: three fully-dressed use cases, each with at least two alternative flows.

8

Finish the domain model

10 minutes · at home

Check every class against the FRs: which requirement needs it? Delete classes nobody needs; add the one a use case mentions. Multiplicities at both ends of every line. If you used Mermaid, open the file on the hosting site and confirm the diagram is drawn; if not, export a PNG from the Mermaid Live Editor8 and commit the image.

Done when: every class justified by an FR; the diagram is visible on the hosting site.

9

Traceability matrix and the two estimates

15 minutes · at home

Fill the matrix — one row per FR: FR · user story · use case · test (empty until Brick 7). An FR with an empty cell is either missing a source (write one) or does not belong (delete it). Then recount the function points carefully with a second person or a second tool, and write one comparison sentence against Brick 3: about 50 lines of code per function point for a typical web language → the lines your FP count implies, versus the Brick 3 size list, and which number you trust more, and why.

Done when: a complete matrix; UFP, FP and the comparison sentence.

10

Commit, tag, push, post

10 minutes · at home

git push does not send tags — push each tag by name.1 Optional first version for feedback by Sunday, October 25, 23:59: block5-draft. Graded version, tagged last, by Sunday, December 20, 2026, 23:59: block5. Moved the file after tagging? git tag -f block5 then git push --force origin block5. Check the tag on the hosting site2, then post the repository link and the tag on the LMS (Learning Management System).

git add docs/
git commit -m "Brick 5: SRS-Lite, use-case model, domain model, traceability, FP count"

Done when: tag visible online; link and tag posted on the LMS.

11

Read and memorise

10 minutes · at home

Pressman & Maxim, 9th edition — chapters 7 and 8 for the parts you did not use today, the function-point pages of chapter 25; the flash-cards of the week. Optional, never graded: the two function-point exercises in /docs/numbers.md. If you are past the hour, stop: what is missing becomes a question for the coached Studio of October 27.

Done when: the hour is over.

Your own tool — a function-point counter in 20 lines

The lab says every tool is open, and that the best tool is one you build. Here is a complete, runnable example in Python6: one list of elements, one loop, the course's weights. Copy it, edit the list for your product, run it with python3 fp_count.py, and put the output in section 5 of your file — then commit the script as your team's tool. Every line has a comment; make sure every member can explain every line (the AI-tools rule applies to scripts too).

# fp_count.py — a tiny function-point counter you can keep in /docs/tools/
# Weights of the course's simplified method (average complexity).
WEIGHTS = {"EI": 4, "EO": 5, "EQ": 4, "ILF": 10, "EIF": 7}

# One line per element: (kind, name). Edit this list for your product.
elements = [
    ("EI", "place order"), ("EI", "register"), ("EI", "update menu item"), ("EI", "mark order ready"),
    ("EO", "confirmation with pick-up number"), ("EO", "end-of-day summary"),
    ("EQ", "view today's menu"), ("EQ", "check order status"), ("EQ", "view my past orders"),
    ("ILF", "Order"), ("ILF", "MenuItem"), ("ILF", "Student"),
    ("EIF", "campus directory (login)"),
]

sum_f = 35  # sum of the 14 influence factors; 35 -> factor 1.00

ufp = 0
for kind in WEIGHTS:                                   # one line per category
    n = sum(1 for k, _ in elements if k == kind)       # how many of this kind
    print(f"{kind:4} {n:2} x {WEIGHTS[kind]:2} = {n * WEIGHTS[kind]:3}")
    ufp += n * WEIGHTS[kind]
fp = ufp * (0.65 + 0.01 * sum_f)
print(f"UFP = {ufp}")
print(f"FP  = {ufp} x (0.65 + 0.01 x {sum_f}) = {fp:.1f}")

Expected output for the QueueLess example: EI 4 × 4 = 16 · EO 2 × 5 = 10 · EQ 3 × 4 = 12 · ILF 3 × 10 = 30 · EIF 1 × 7 = 7 · UFP = 75 · FP = 75.0. A spreadsheet with five rows does the same job; so does a calculator and a pencil.

Version notes — where a newer version may look different

  1. Git 2.56.0 (released September 28, 2026) is what the terminal animation imitates. Newer versions may word their messages differently; the commands add, commit, push, tag and push origin ⟨tag⟩ have not changed in years and are described in the Pro Git chapter Tagging.
  2. Hosting-site menus move. On GitHub the tag list is reached through Releases → Tags at the time of writing; if your site shows it elsewhere, search its documentation for “tags” — GitHub Docs — Viewing tags.
  3. Mermaid 12.1. The class diagram in the template uses syntax that has been stable for years and is drawn by GitHub inside Markdown (GitHub Docs — Creating diagrams). The use-case diagram is new in Mermaid 12 and still carries the keyword usecase-beta (Mermaid — Use case diagrams): a hosting site running an older Mermaid will not draw it, and its look may change when it leaves beta. Check the version your site runs with a mermaid block containing the single word info; if the diagram does not render, export a PNG from the Live Editor and commit the image. The template's two diagrams were rendered with Mermaid 12.1.0 on October 12, 2026.
  4. Visual Studio Code 1.141 (October 2026) ships a new version every month; menus and the Markdown preview may differ slightly from any description. Any editor is fine.
  5. draw.io and Excalidraw are web applications that change their look without version numbers; the shapes you need (stick figure, ellipse, rectangle, line) exist in every version. A photographed paper sketch is just as acceptable.
  6. Python 3.14 (3.14.4 was the latest release on October 12, 2026; 3.15 is expected this autumn). The example script uses nothing newer than Python 3.6 (f-strings), so it runs on any current version.
  7. Function-point weights. The course uses a simplified method with average weights (4 · 5 · 4 · 10 · 7) and ΣF = 35. The full counting practices maintained by the IFPUG (International Function Point Users Group) rate each element's complexity (low / average / high) and give different weights per level, so a professional count of the same product can differ from yours. Say which method you used.
  8. Mermaid Live Editor. The export menu (PNG / SVG) has moved between versions of the editor; look for “Actions” or “Export” in the side panel — mermaid.live.
